extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism; students of literature; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the quality of philosophical prose and novels (style, argument, moral practicability, invention, characterization, descriptive power) as discussed in a 19th-century literary-critical essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness versus valuation (Bentham's topicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It includes every thing; but it includes every thing alike. It is rather like an inventory, than a valuation of different arguments. Every possible suggestion finds a place, so that the mind is distracted as much as enlightened by this perplexing accuracy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating all points with equal weight; when summing up, consider the amount/importance of items, not merely the number. Do not let exhaustive listing obscure judgement about what matters most; exceptions should not be made as important as the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technicality and accessibility of manner
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is a technicality of manner, which renders his writings of more value to the professional inquirer than to the general reader...He writes a language of his own, that darkens knowledge.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear, accessible expression over specialised 'cipher' language. Writing aimed at broader readership should avoid dense professional jargon that 'darkens knowledge' and places the work 'almost out of the reach' of general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence construction and perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The construction of his sentences is a curious frame-work with pegs and hooks to hang his thoughts upon...a barbarous philosophical jargon, with all the repetitions, parentheses, formalities, uncouth nomenclature and verbiage of law-Latin.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sentence structures that enhance readability and clarity; avoid excessively long, parenthetical, or hook-laden periods that obscure meaning. Strive for perspicuity so the reader can 'pick out' the acuteness and meaning without effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-compression and overrating trivial details
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mr. Bentham writes as if he was allowed but a single sentence to express his whole view of a subject in, and as if, should he omit a single circumstance or step of the argument, it would be lost to the world for ever...This is over-rating the importance of our own discoveries, and mistaking the nature and object of language altogether.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cram an entire argument into one convoluted sentence or treat every minor point as indispensable. Balance completeness with clearness; understand that omission does not imply irretrievability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve natural humour and simple style
rubrics_metrics.description: “His admirable little work On Usury...is clear, easy, and vigorous. But Mr. Bentham has shut himself up since then...and has endeavoured to overlay his natural humour, sense, spirit, and style, with the dust and cobwebs of an obscure solitude.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the writer's natural voice, humour, and simplicity rather than allowing solitude or excessive technicality to obscure earlier clarity and vigour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of perspective versus narrow utility-focus
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is one of those who prefer the artificial to the natural in most things, and think the mind of man omnipotent. He has a great contempt for out-of-door prospects, for green fields and trees, and is for referring every thing to Utility. There is a little narrowness in this...if all the sources of satisfaction are taken away, what is to become of utility itself?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing evaluation or moral worth solely to a single metric (e.g., Utility). Allow for multiple sources of satisfaction and values; ensure philosophical or critical perspective retains universality and does not become unduly narrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicability and realism of moral prescriptions (Godwin)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fault, then, of Mr. Godwin's philosophy, in one word, was too much ambition...he raided the standard of morality above the reach of humanity...by directing virtue to the most airy and romantic heights, made her path dangerous, solitary, and impracticable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure moral or philosophical systems are practicable for ordinary human beings. Do not convert extreme or exceptional prescriptions into everyday rules; consider human limitations and the real-world applicability of principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between reason and sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mr. Godwin's definition of morals was the same as the admired one of law, reason 'without passion'; but...there was danger that the unseasoned novice might substitute some pragmatical conceit of his own for the rule of right reason, and mistake a heartless indifference for a superiority to more natural and generous feelings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy and moral argument should balance rational analysis with human affections and sentiments; reason alone, without regard to feeling, can lead to sterile or inhumane prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of human affections and social ties
rubrics_metrics.description: “He absolves man from the gross and narrow ties of sense, custom, authority, private and local attachment...Gratitude, promises, friendship, family affection give way...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral theories by how they treat social bonds, promises, gratitude, and family ties. Complete abstraction from these auxiliary aids risks producing impractical or socially destructive prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of extreme testing to find limits (intellectual probing)
rubrics_metrics.description: “His grand work is (at least) an experimentum cruets to show the weak sides and imperfections of human reason as the sole law of human action...By overshooting the mark...he has pointed out the limit or line of separation, between what is practicable and what is barely conceivable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using rigorous, extreme reasoning can be valuable to reveal the limits and weak points of doctrines, even if the thinker 'overshoots'—this discovery of limits is an intellectual service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention and execution (novel-writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Caleb Williams and St. Leon are two of the most splendid and impressive works of the imagination...a master-piece, both as to invention and execution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge fiction by originality of idea (invention) and the skill with which it is realized (execution). Both novelty and craftsmanship matter in assessing a novel's merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character creation and interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: “Perhaps the art with which these two characters are contrived to relieve and set off each other, has never been surpassed...the restless and inquisitive spirit of Caleb Williams...haunts the latter like a second conscience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how characters are constructed and how they interact to illuminate each other and the themes; contrasting and complementary characterization strengthens dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement and memorability
rubrics_metrics.description: “We conceive no one ever began Caleb Williams that did not read it through: no one that ever read it could possibly forget it...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful work should engross the reader (compel them to continue) and leave a lasting impression; consider pacing, suspense, and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive imagery and immersive identification
rubrics_metrics.description: “St. Leon...is set off by a more gorgeous and flowing eloquence, and by a crown of preternatural imagery...the beauty and the charm of Mr. Godwin's descriptions that the reader identifies himself with the author; and the secret of this is, that the author has identified himself with his personages.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong, vivid description that springs from the author's identification with characters produces reader identification and immersion; poetic or eloquent imagery can enhance emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality versus patch-work borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no look of patch-work and plagiarism...no tracery-work from worm-eaten manuscripts, from forgotten chronicles, nor piecing out of vague traditions...Here all is clearly made out with strokes of the pencil, by fair, not by factitious means.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that show authentic invention and internal creation over those that feel pieced together from borrowed fragments or mere pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and avoidance of monotony
rubrics_metrics.description: “He who draws upon his own resources, easily comes to an end of his wealth...Mr. Godwin, in all his writings, dwells upon one idea or exclusive view of a subject...and makes up by the force of style and continuity of feeling for what he wants in variety of incident or ease of manner.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against monotony by introducing variety in incident, tone, and perspective; even highly original writers should strive for variety to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tone; avoid mawkishness or morbidity
rubrics_metrics.description: “This necessary defect is observable in his best works, and is still more so in Fleetwood and Mandeville; the one of which, compared with his more admired performances, is mawkish, and the other morbid.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tone suits subject and audience; excessive sentimentality (mawkishness) or unhealthy morbidity weakens effect and can undermine artistic merit.
